body:
Last night on Predictable, we spent a lot of time on something we’ve been trying to hammer home since this show launched: The biggest value in prediction markets usually comes 
before
 the headlines catch up.
That’s exactly what happened with Thomas Massie.
If you just parachuted into the race over the past few days, you probably saw what everyone else saw:
a bunch of “tied” polls
some Massie-friendly numbers
conservatives online confidently saying he’d survive
But if you’d been following the market movement with us over the past couple weeks, you could already see the direction this thing was heading.
Not certainty. Not inevitability. But movement.
And that’s really the edge prediction markets can give you.
The Polls Weren’t Actually Saying What People Thought They Were Saying
One of the big points Stu walked through on the show was how misleading polling averages can become if you don’t actually look underneath them.
At a quick glance, the race looked close.
But once you separated out the actual pollsters, the picture changed pretty fast.
A lot of the strongest Massie numbers came from Big Data Poll. And even 
those
 polls showed momentum moving toward Ed Gallehrain late in the race.
Then you looked at the other firms:
Quantus: Gallehrain +8
SoCal: Gallehrain +7
Greyhouse: Gallehrain +7
At that point, the market wasn’t reacting emotionally anymore.
It was repricing the race.
And if you were paying attention to Predictable, you were seeing that happen in real time while a lot of the broader political conversation was still treating this as “Massie probably hangs on.”
This Was Never Just a Normal Trump Endorsement
Another thing we talked about repeatedly: There’s a difference between Trump endorsing someone… and Trump deciding he personally wants someone removed from office.
Those are two different political forces.
Massie wasn’t dealing with a casual endorsement. He was dealing with what Stu jokingly described as Trump’s “hibachi-level obsession.” The money understood that.
Over $32 million flooded into this race. Outside groups mobilized. The entire environment around the election changed. And the market started reflecting that shift long before most people were ready to admit the race had fundamentally changed.
This Is Why We Focus So Much On Process
One thing we try to avoid on Predictable is pretending every position is some guaranteed lock. Politics doesn’t work that way. But the process matters.
The goal is to recognize when the environment is changing 
before
 everyone suddenly agrees it changed. That’s where the value usually is. By the time Gallehrain moved into the 60-cent range on Kalshi, a lot of the easiest value had already disappeared.
That doesn’t mean the market was “finished.” It just means the early signal had already done a lot of the work. And honestly, the Massie race became one of the clearest examples we’ve had so far of why this show exists in the first place.
The full episode also dives into:
how local races create weird market inefficiencies
why live election-night swings can create sudden opportunities
why Spencer Pratt may still be undervalued in Los Angeles
and how to think about stacking smaller gains while preparing for the midterms
If you’ve been trying to understand how prediction markets actually work in practice — not just theory — this was a really good episode to watch.
